summary: This informational RFC gives a methodology for measuring how much monitoring and exporting IP flow records slows a network device. It adds the rate at which flows are created, expired and exported as a performance metric alongside throughput.

plainLanguage.summary: If a worker has to count and report each passing car, they can get slower. This describes how to measure that slowdown.

subtitle: Measuring how much network monitoring slows down a router

tldr.problem: Network operators want to monitor traffic by tracking flows (conversations between IP addresses and ports) and exporting that data, but they do not know how much this monitoring will slow down their routers or reduce packet throughput.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC provides a standardized methodology for measuring the maximum rate at which a router can monitor and export flow records without losing packets or dropping flow information. It extends RFC 2544 (router benchmarking) to account for the overhead of flow monitoring.
tldr.outcome: Operators can compare flow monitoring performance across different routers and vendors, and understand the performance cost of different monitoring configurations.

today: RFC 6645 is Informational and provides the standard methodology for benchmarking flow monitoring performance. It extends RFC 2544 and is used by vendors to publish performance data and by operators to evaluate equipment purchases. The method remains current as IPFIX continues to be the standard export protocol.

sections.title: Flow Monitoring and Its Cost
sections.content:
IP Flow Monitoring means a router watches packets passing through it, groups them into conversations (flows) based on source address, destination address, port numbers, and other fields, and maintains counters for each flow (how many packets, how many bytes). Periodically, the router exports these flow records to a collector for analysis. This is widely used in service provider and enterprise networks for traffic engineering, capacity planning, billing, and security.

But monitoring is not free. A router must allocate memory for a cache of active flows, process each packet to match it to a flow, update counters, check for flow timeouts, and format and export records. This consumes CPU, memory, and I/O resources that could otherwise forward packets. Network operators need to know how much monitoring will impact their forwarding performance before they deploy it.
sections.plainLanguage: Flow monitoring is like a guard counting people walking through a door. Counting takes effort and the guard might slow down the line. This document says how to measure that slowdown.

sections.title: The Measurement Challenge
sections.content:
A network device with flow monitoring enabled has two independent functional blocks: the Forwarding Plane, which decides where each packet should go, and the Monitoring Plane, which analyzes traffic and exports flows. Both compete for the device's resources. The forwarding plane performance is measured by throughput (packets per second) as defined in RFC 2544. The monitoring plane performance is measured by Flow Export Rate (how many flow records per second the device can export without losing information).

The key insight is that these two planes must be measured together when both are present. A device might forward packets at full rate while exporting very few flows, or export many flows while forwarding fewer packets. The challenge is to find the point where the device reaches its limit in one or both planes, measuring whether it drops packets, loses flow records, or corrupts flow information.
sections.plainLanguage: A router has two jobs: forward packets and export flow records. Both need resources. We need to measure how fast it can do both before something breaks.

sections.title: How to Set Up the Test
sections.content:
The measurement setup is based on RFC 2544's standard topology: a test device sends traffic through the router under test, and a receiver verifies what comes out. A new addition is a Collector that captures flow export data sent by the router. The router must have sufficient memory for a flow cache, and the export link must have enough bandwidth so it is not a bottleneck.

The router's flow monitoring configuration is critical: how large is the flow cache, what timeout values are used (how long until an idle flow is forgotten or an active flow is forced to expire), which packet fields are flow keys (used to group packets into flows), and which export protocol is used (IPFIX is preferred for standardization). All these parameters must be documented in the measurement report so results can be compared fairly across different tests and vendors.
sections.plainLanguage: Send test traffic through the router, collect the flow export data it produces, and measure both the forwarded packets and the exported flows. Write down all the router settings so the test can be repeated.

sections.title: The Key Metric: Flow Monitoring Throughput
sections.content:
Flow Monitoring Throughput is the maximum number of flow records per second that a router can export without losing a single flow record or packet. This is the benchmark metric for the monitoring plane. It captures the point at which the router's resources are fully consumed.

To measure it, test traffic is sent with a new flow for every packet (by varying the source and destination IP addresses). This creates the maximum rate of flow creation, which exercises the monitoring plane hardest. The test increases traffic rate using a binary search algorithm (standard in RFC 2544) until either flow information is lost or the forwarding plane starts dropping packets. The rate at which this happens is the Flow Monitoring Throughput. The measurement is repeated at different frame sizes and traffic patterns to fully characterize the device.
sections.plainLanguage: Send traffic where every packet is a different conversation. Keep increasing the speed until the router loses track of a conversation or drops a packet. That speed is the limit.

sections.title: Reporting Results and Comparing Devices
sections.content:
A complete measurement report must document the device under test, the exact topology, all router configuration (cache size, timeouts, flow keys, export protocol and transport layer), the test traffic configuration (packet rates, frame sizes, how flow keys were varied), and the results (the flow export rates measured and at what point the device failed). The report should also note any internal metrics gathered, such as CPU load or memory utilization, as these help explain the results.

Only measurements with identical configurations should be compared. A device tested with large flow cache and small timeout values will have different results than one with a tiny cache and large timeouts, even if the device hardware is identical. Similarly, different flow key definitions, export protocols, and packet sizes all affect the results. This is why detailed documentation is essential: without it, comparing two vendors' claims is impossible.
sections.plainLanguage: Write down everything: the router, the settings, the test, and where it broke. Only compare tests with the same settings. Otherwise it's like comparing one car's speed on a highway and another car's speed in town.

sections.title: What Devices Can Be Tested
sections.content:
This methodology applies to any network device that implements the IPFIX architecture defined in RFC 5470: routers, switches, and monitoring appliances that do not forward packets but observe traffic. The methodology is the same for IPv4, IPv6, and MPLS traffic, though the flow keys and packet fields differ. Some devices may not support flow monitoring of certain traffic types, in which case testing is simply restricted to what the device supports.

The methodology does not measure the collector's performance (how fast it can process received flow records). Rather, it ensures the collector has sufficient resources so it is not the bottleneck during measurement. This isolates the router's performance from collector limitations, allowing fair comparison of different routers.
sections.plainLanguage: This method works for routers, switches, and dedicated monitoring boxes. You can test IPv4, IPv6, or MPLS traffic. As long as the collector doesn't slow things down, the results are about the router.
